person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: whether primary and non-primary auditory cortex encode the temporal shape of the sound envelope on different time scales
span.quote: We find response durations and optimal time constants for discriminating sound envelope shape increase in rank order with: A1 < VAF < cSRAF. Accordingly, sustained spiking is more prominent and results in more robust sound discrimination in non-primary cortex versus A1.

span.label: whether a functional hierarchy of the kind established in vision for receptive field size exists in audition along the time axis instead
span.quote: Functional hierarchies in the visual cortices support the concept that classification of visual objects requires successive cortical stages of processing including a progressive increase in classical receptive field size. The present study is significant as it supports the idea that a similar progression exists in auditory cortices in the time domain. We demonstrate for the first time that three cortices provide temporal spiking patterns for robust temporal envelope shape discrimination but only the ventral non-primary cortices do so on long time scales.

span.label: response duration and the integration time constant that best discriminates sound shape both increase in rank order A1 < VAF < cSRAF, so the non-primary fields carry the same cue on a longer time scale
span.quote: We find response durations and optimal time constants for discriminating sound envelope shape increase in rank order with: A1 < VAF < cSRAF. Accordingly, sustained spiking is more prominent and results in more robust sound discrimination in non-primary cortex versus A1.

span.label: existence
span.quote: We find response durations and optimal time constants for discriminating sound envelope shape increase in rank order with: A1 < VAF < cSRAF.

span.label: temporal coding of sound envelope shape across auditory cortical fields
span.quote: Here, we examine the possibility that A1, VAF, and cSRAF could provide unique temporal codes for discriminating and classifying sound based on the temporal shape of the sound envelope.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: Data were collected from 223 single neurons from 16 male Brown Norway rats.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Longer sustained responses in ventral non-primary cortex require a downstream reader to integrate over a longer time constant, which is what produces the hierarchy of optimal time scales
span.quote: The longer time scales needed for optimal discrimination in VAF and cSRAF suggest the longer response durations ( Fig. 2 D ) contribute to sound discrimination.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Pooling across neurons averages out the timing jitter of individual spike trains, restoring classification accuracy in temporally imprecise fields
span.quote: The pooling advantage in general is consistent with the proposition that pooling activity of groups of neurons can compensate for spike train imprecision in individual neurons

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Field-specific thalamocortical pathways impose a time-frequency trade-off, buying A1 its temporal resolution at the cost of spectral resolution and vice versa for non-primary fields
span.quote: It is possible these specializations reflect time-frequency tradeoffs in sound processing where A1, and its corresponding thalamocortical pathway, have superior temporal resolution at the expense of spectral resolution.

span.label: longer response durations in the ventral fields give a downstream reader more time to integrate, so the time constant that best discriminates sound shape is longer there
span.quote: A1 has optimal time constants <25 ms on average for sound shape f c between 6 and 16 Hz; whereas, cSRAF has optimal time constants >35 ms for these same sounds ( Fig. 5 H , asterisks; for A1 vs cSRAF: Student's t test, p < 0.001; Wilcoxon rank-sum, p < 0.01). The longer time scales needed for optimal discrimination in VAF and cSRAF suggest the longer response durations ( Fig. 2 D ) contribute to sound discrimination. For the range of sound shapes where discrimination is near maximum, time constants are rank ordered and increasing with: A1 < VAF < cSRAF (i.e., for f c between 6 and 16 Hz, Wilcoxon rank-sum, p < 0.01).

span.label: onset spikes carry most of the discrimination in every field, and what is left after they are removed is what separates the fields - the sustained spikes work better in VAF and cSRAF
span.quote: Discrimination matrices illustrate that all three cortical fields discriminate sound shape well with onset spikes alone for many pairwise sound comparisons ( Fig. 7 A–C , yellow, orange, red voxels). Using onset spikes alone, sound discrimination performance decreases significantly with increasing sound f c ( F (8,1323) = 141.32, p < 0.001, two-way ANOVA) in all three cortical fields ( Fig. 7 D ). In all three cortical fields, discrimination performance is generally lower when only the secondary spikes are used to estimate sound shape discrimination ( Fig. 7 E–G vs A–C ). However, VAF and cSRAF outperform A1 when only these secondary spikes are used ( Fig. 7 H , asterisks). These results support the idea that onset responses strongly contribute to neural discrimination of sound shape in all cortical fields; whereas, sustained responses provide more effective discrimination in non-primary cortices, VAF and cSRAF.

span.label: and pooling compensates for imprecision - performance rises 2 to 3 fold over the average single neuron, with half maximal performance reached from fewer than 10 neurons
span.quote: The pooling advantage in general is consistent with the proposition that pooling activity of groups of neurons can compensate for spike train imprecision in individual neurons ( Zohary et al., 1994 ; Geffen et al., 2009 ; Bizley et al., 2010 ; Schneider and Woolley, 2010 ; Carruthers et al., 2015 ). The new twist in the present study is that pooling is also important for robust temporal-code-based sound classification in non-primary cortices like cSRAF, a region with temporally sluggish and imprecise responses that are longer in response duration

span.label: we CANNOT DISAMBIGUATE potential neural codes for sound burst slope versus duration AS THESE CUES COVARY IN OUR SOUNDS
span.quote: Here we cannot disambiguate potential neural codes for sound burst slope versus duration as these cues covary in our sounds (see Materials and Methods).

span.label: we HOLD SPECTRAL AND SPATIAL CUES CONSTANT to examine neural coding of temporal cues in the sound envelope independently
span.quote: In the present study, we hold spectral and spatial cues constant to examine neural coding of temporal cues in the sound envelope independently.

span.label: TWO CANDIDATE CODES THAT THIS DESIGN CANNOT SEPARATE, SAID OUT LOUD: we CANNOT DISAMBIGUATE potential neural codes for sound burst slope versus duration AS THESE CUES COVARY IN OUR SOUNDS
span.quote: Here we cannot disambiguate potential neural codes for sound burst slope versus duration as these cues covary in our sounds (see Materials and Methods). However, these results raise the intriguing possibility that there are unique neural codes for the slope versus duration of a sound burst and that non-primary cortices are more sensitive to the latter.

span.label: the spike-distance metric is biased at long time constants, and the fix is SYNTHETIC DATA - a periodic spike train with matched temporal statistics, extended to 100 s, standing in for the recording
span.quote: As τ approaches the total length of the spike train (2 s), the spike distance is biased and yields large values. When comparing two spike trains, slight difference in the spike rate will contribute to a large spike-distance metric because there is not enough time for the exponential function to decay. To minimize this confound, we extended the length of spike train by synthesizing a periodic spike train with matched temporal statistics to the measured data ( Zheng and Escabí, 2008 ). For each cycle of the synthetic periodic spike train, both the spike rate and spike times were randomly sampled from the original spike train. This process was repeated to generate periodic spike trains with durations of 100 s.

span.label: the classifier assumes response bins from different neurons are INDEPENDENT, which the paper states as a design property rather than as a fact about the brain
span.quote: By design, the naive Bayes classifier treats responses bins from different neurons as if they are independent. This property allows the classifier to take advantage of any independent and nonredundant responses within the population to build more robust classification.

span.label: the first 500 ms of every spike train is discarded, so every number here is about the ADAPTED STEADY-STATE segment and not about the response to a sound that has just begun
span.quote: For all data analyses, the first 500 ms was removed from each spike train to restrict analysis to the adapted steady-state segments of the neural responses.

span.label: future exploration will be needed to determine whether classification is even more robust when spectral, temporal and spatial features are COMBINED, and WHEN ANIMALS ARE ATTENDING during a behavioral task, AS HAPPENS IN NATURAL SETTINGS
span.quote: Future exploration will be needed to determine whether neuronal classification of sound's temporal shape is even more robust in non-primary auditory cortices when spectral, temporal and spatial features are combined ( Carruthers et al., 2015 ; Engineer et al., 2015 ; Town et al., 2017 ) and when animals are attending during a behavioral tasks ( von Trapp et al., 2016 ), as happens in natural settings.

span.label: a Bernoulli Naive Bayes classifier of McCallum and Nigam 1998, used to READ OUT THE SPIKE TRAINS from individual neurons and CATEGORIZE THE SOUND SHAPE
span.quote: A Bernoulli Naive Bayes classifier ( McCallum and Nigam, 1998 ) is used to read out the spike trains from individual neurons to categorize the sound shape.

span.label: the sensitivity index d-prime, a measure of behavioural discriminability, is repurposed to normalize a spike-train distance so that neural discrimination is expressed on a behavioural scale
span.quote: The distance metric was normalized by trial variances to compute a sensitivity index or discrimination index as commonly used to measure behavioral discriminability

span.label: the functional hierarchy of successive stages with progressively larger receptive fields, carried from space into the time axis
span.quote: Functional hierarchies in the visual cortices support the concept that classification of visual objects requires successive cortical stages of processing including a progressive increase in classical receptive field size. The present study is significant as it supports the idea that a similar progression exists in auditory cortices in the time domain. We demonstrate for the first time that three cortices provide temporal spiking patterns for robust temporal envelope shape discrimination but only the ventral non-primary cortices do so on long time scales.

span.label: an exponential-kernel spike distance, normalized by trial variance so that it reads as a sensitivity index
span.quote: The exponential time constant, τ, determines the temporal resolution or integration time of the distance metric. For large values of τ, the signals being compared contain mostly slow fluctuations in the spike rate ( Fig. 3 E , F ). For small τ, the spike distance metric is sensitive to the precise timing of spikes. We varied τ in 16 logarithmic intervals from 1 to 256 ms, and computed discrimination index ( D′ ) for each τ and each reference sound ( Fig. 4 ; reference sound f c = 64 Hz) and then determined the time constant (τ or tau) that yields the optimal (aka, maximal) sound discrimination ( Fig. 4 , asterisks). The same approach was used for all possible sound pairings and sound references and discrimination indices are plotted in a matrix ( Fig. 5 ). A discrimination index of zero was obtained when the two response conditions were identical (aka, sound vs itself) and plotted on the diagonal of the corresponding discrimination index matrix ( Fig. 5 , diagonal cells). Using a τ of 256 ms, the time constant is longer than half of the cycle period (500 ms), and the spike distance is closely related to the difference in the total spike rates. The range of time-constants tested enabled us to test the role precise spike timing at one extreme and the role of slow fluctuations in spike rate at the other extreme might play for neural discrimination of temporal envelope cues.

span.label: a D-prime of 1 corresponds to about 70% accuracy, WHICH IS TYPICALLY CONSIDERED A CRITICAL LIMIT FOR DISCRIMINATING A SIGNAL BEHAVIORALLY
span.quote: Here, a D′ = 1 corresponds ∼70% accuracy, which is typically considered a critical limit for discriminating a signal behaviorally ( von Trapp et al., 2016 ).

span.label: a Bernoulli naive Bayes classifier reading spike trains as bit patterns, with its independence assumption declared and used deliberately
span.quote: By design, the naive Bayes classifier treats responses bins from different neurons as if they are independent. This property allows the classifier to take advantage of any independent and nonredundant responses within the population to build more robust classification.

span.label: the noise carrier varied across trials and across bursts, unfrozen
span.quote: The noise carriers were varied (unfrozen) across trials and for individual sound bursts to remove spectral biases and to prevent repetition of fine-structure temporal patterns. This guarantees that, on average, the only physical cues available to each neuron arise from the temporal envelope.

span.label: spectral and spatial cues held constant across every condition
span.quote: In the present study, we hold spectral and spatial cues constant to examine neural coding of temporal cues in the sound envelope independently.

span.label: each sound discriminated against itself
span.quote: As expected, when the sound shapes being compared are identical (i.e., the sound vs itself), sound discrimination is zero ( Fig. 5 A–C , matrix diagonal, dark blue voxels).

span.label: the spike count distribution tested against a Poisson model before the rate classifier was built on it
span.quote: The spike count distribution p s ( k ) was approximated as a Poisson model because it provided a good fit to spike-rate data ( N = 223, χ 2 (d f =50) < 11.26, p < 0.05, χ 2 test).

span.label: recording depth restricted to 400 to 650 micrometers
span.quote: Data from penetration depths of 400–650 μm relative to the pial surface were included in the present study, as this corresponds to layer 4 where ventral division auditory thalamic neurons project

span.label: discrimination
span.quote: Discrimination performance drops ( p < 0.05, f c ( F (8,1323) = 44.8, two-way ANOVA) for sounds with half-durations shorter than 28 ms (shape f c ≥ 8 Hz) when the reference sound half-duration is 2 ms ( f c of 64 Hz) suggesting a half-resolution limit on the order of 20 ms

span.label: duration
span.quote: Discrimination performance drops ( p < 0.05, f c ( F (8,1323) = 44.8, two-way ANOVA) for sounds with half-durations shorter than 28 ms (shape f c ≥ 8 Hz) when the reference sound half-duration is 2 ms ( f c of 64 Hz) suggesting a half-resolution limit on the order of 20 ms

span.label: A HIERARCHY OF TIME SCALES: response durations and optimal time constants for discriminating sound envelope shape INCREASE IN RANK ORDER WITH A1 < VAF < cSRAF, so sustained spiking is more prominent and discrimination more robust in NON-PRIMARY cortex
span.quote: We find response durations and optimal time constants for discriminating sound envelope shape increase in rank order with: A1 < VAF < cSRAF. Accordingly, sustained spiking is more prominent and results in more robust sound discrimination in non-primary cortex versus A1.

span.label: AND THE RANK ORDER REVERSES WITH THE MEASURE: A1 and VAF have significantly HIGHER mean discrimination than cSRAF across all 45 pairs - CONVERSELY cSRAF is better across 30 pairwise comparisons when the sound is slower than 11 Hz. The same three fields, opposite orders, one figure apart
span.quote: Though the differences are small, A1 and VAF have significantly higher mean discrimination than cSRAF averaged across all 45 pairwise discriminations ( Fig. 5 A–C ). Conversely, cSRAF neurons are marginally better at discriminating across 30 pairwise sound comparisons when sound burst f c is <11 Hz ( Fig. 5 A–C ; f c < 11 Hz) and corresponding sound burst half-duration is >14 ms.

span.label: and reverses again by task: A1 AND VAF OUTPERFORM cSRAF in 10 alternative forced choice classification, where the ranking A1 > VAF > cSRAF is the INVERSE of the time-scale ranking
span.quote: Together these results indicate that spike-timing patterns provide a better signal than spike-rate patterns for classifying sound shape in primary and non-primary cortices. Furthermore, A1 and VAF outperform cSRAF in 10 alternative forced choice classification scenarios.

span.label: and once more by stimulus, inside the pooling analysis: the effect of pooling was GREATER ON AVERAGE IN A1 than in cSRAF, HOWEVER the benefit was GREATER IN cSRAF for two of the longest duration sound bursts - THE ADVANTAGES OF POOLING VARY WITH THE TIME SCALE OF THE SOUND
span.quote: The effect of pooling on classification performance was greater on average in A1 than in cSRAF ( Table 2 , far right column); however, the benefit of pooling was greater in cSRAF for two of the longest duration sound bursts ( Table 2 ; f c of 2 and 8 Hz). These results indicate that the advantages of pooling vary with the time scale of the sound and the response as well as across cortical fields.

span.label: with the inverse relation stated as the finding rather than as a caveat: the ability to classify 10 sound shapes IS INVERSELY RELATED to the temporal imprecision of cortical responses, A1 > VAF > cSRAF - the field that discriminates on the longest time scale classifies worst
span.quote: Here, we provide additional evidence that the ability to classify 10 sound shapes with spike-timing pattern is inversely related to the temporal imprecision of cortical responses with: A1 > VAF > cSRAF. Thus, cSRAF typically has weak onset and longer duration responses with correspondingly less accurate sound classification performance with the temporal-code-based classifier ( Fig. 8 P , solid lines). Conversely, cSRAF has a slightly more robust performance with the rate-code-based classifier

span.label: THE OPERATIONAL DEFINITION OF `ONSET SPIKE` IS A WINDOW THAT DIFFERS EIGHTFOLD BETWEEN THE FIELDS BEING COMPARED: the onset response time window is 29.6 ms for A1 and 180.7 ms for cSRAF at the slowest sound, and a single window is measured PER CONDITION AND PER REGION

and the paper says so plainly: onset response time windows VARY WITH SOUND BURST HALF-DURATION AND SLOPE as determined by the sound shaping filter, and are given FOR EACH SOUND BURST VARIATION AND CORTICAL FIELD
span.quote: Onset response time windows, determined as described in Materials and Methods, vary with sound burst half-duration and slope as determined by the sound shaping filter ( f c ). Onset response times are given for each sound burst variation and cortical field.

span.label: A TERM REDEFINED MID-PAPER, EXPLICITLY: onset spikes are a MIXTURE of stimulus-evoked and spontaneous activity, a subset is categorised as spontaneous BY RANDOM SAMPLING against a Poisson criterion, and IN THE REMAINDER OF THIS MANUSCRIPT WE USE THE TERM ONSET SPIKES TO DENOTE THE EVOKED ONSET SPIKES ONLY
span.quote: Onset spikes are composed of a mixture of both stimulus-evoked and spontaneous activity. To estimate the contribution of both sources of spiking, we measured the baseline spiking rate from a 50 ms window centered a half cycle before the stimulus peak, and assumed the baseline spike rate during the onset window varied about the mean spontaneous rate according to a Poisson distribution. Onset spike rates exceeding the 0.001% criterion level of this distribution were therefore assumed to include an additional contribution of evoked activity above the spontaneous rate. Accordingly, we categorized a subset of the onset spikes as spontaneous, by randomly sampling from the onset spikes with a spike rate up to the 0.001% criterion level. All remaining spikes were considered evoked onset spikes. Finally, the spontaneous onset spikes were added to the secondary spike train. In the remainder of this manuscript, we use the term “onset” spikes to denote the evoked onset spikes only.

span.label: SYNTHETIC DATA INSIDE THE MEASUREMENT CHAIN, DECLARED: as the time constant approaches the length of the spike train THE SPIKE DISTANCE IS BIASED, so the spike train was EXTENDED BY SYNTHESIZING a periodic spike train WITH MATCHED TEMPORAL STATISTICS, sampling rate and times from the original, out to 100 s
span.quote: As τ approaches the total length of the spike train (2 s), the spike distance is biased and yields large values. When comparing two spike trains, slight difference in the spike rate will contribute to a large spike-distance metric because there is not enough time for the exponential function to decay. To minimize this confound, we extended the length of spike train by synthesizing a periodic spike train with matched temporal statistics to the measured data ( Zheng and Escabí, 2008 ). For each cycle of the synthetic periodic spike train, both the spike rate and spike times were randomly sampled from the original spike train. This process was repeated to generate periodic spike trains with durations of 100 s.

span.label: TWO CANDIDATE CODES THIS DESIGN CANNOT SEPARATE: we CANNOT DISAMBIGUATE potential neural codes for sound burst slope versus duration AS THESE CUES COVARY IN OUR SOUNDS - and the untestable possibility is still stated, that non-primary cortices are more sensitive to duration
span.quote: Here we cannot disambiguate potential neural codes for sound burst slope versus duration as these cues covary in our sounds (see Materials and Methods). However, these results raise the intriguing possibility that there are unique neural codes for the slope versus duration of a sound burst and that non-primary cortices are more sensitive to the latter.

span.label: an imported threshold that gives the index its meaning: a D-prime of 1 corresponds to about 70% accuracy, WHICH IS TYPICALLY CONSIDERED A CRITICAL LIMIT for discriminating a signal behaviorally - a behavioral criterion borrowed to read a number computed from spikes
span.quote: Here, a D′ = 1 corresponds ∼70% accuracy, which is typically considered a critical limit for discriminating a signal behaviorally ( von Trapp et al., 2016 ).

span.label: an assumption declared and then used as a feature: the naive Bayes classifier TREATS RESPONSE BINS FROM DIFFERENT NEURONS AS IF THEY ARE INDEPENDENT, which ALLOWS THE CLASSIFIER TO TAKE ADVANTAGE OF any independent and nonredundant responses
span.quote: By design, the naive Bayes classifier treats responses bins from different neurons as if they are independent. This property allows the classifier to take advantage of any independent and nonredundant responses within the population to build more robust classification.

span.label: and a scope restriction that is easy to miss: THE FIRST 500 ms WAS REMOVED FROM EACH SPIKE TRAIN to restrict analysis to the ADAPTED STEADY-STATE segments
span.quote: For all data analyses, the first 500 ms was removed from each spike train to restrict analysis to the adapted steady-state segments of the neural responses.

span.label: THE PARAMETER IS THE FINDING: the exponential time constant DETERMINES THE TEMPORAL RESOLUTION OR INTEGRATION TIME of the metric, large values leave mostly slow fluctuations in spike rate and small values make it sensitive to precise timing - the range tested is what lets one number stand for two rival codes
span.quote: The exponential time constant, τ, determines the temporal resolution or integration time of the distance metric. For large values of τ, the signals being compared contain mostly slow fluctuations in the spike rate ( Fig. 3 E , F ). For small τ, the spike distance metric is sensitive to the precise timing of spikes. We varied τ in 16 logarithmic intervals from 1 to 256 ms, and computed discrimination index ( D′ ) for each τ and each reference sound ( Fig. 4 ; reference sound f c = 64 Hz) and then determined the time constant (τ or tau) that yields the optimal (aka, maximal) sound discrimination ( Fig. 4 , asterisks). The same approach was used for all possible sound pairings and sound references and discrimination indices are plotted in a matrix ( Fig. 5 ). A discrimination index of zero was obtained when the two response conditions were identical (aka, sound vs itself) and plotted on the diagonal of the corresponding discrimination index matrix ( Fig. 5 , diagonal cells). Using a τ of 256 ms, the time constant is longer than half of the cycle period (500 ms), and the spike distance is closely related to the difference in the total spike rates. The range of time-constants tested enabled us to test the role precise spike timing at one extreme and the role of slow fluctuations in spike rate at the other extreme might play for neural discrimination of temporal envelope cues.

span.label: SPIKE RATE IS NEAR CHANCE AND SAID TO BE SO: all three fields classify with LOW PERFORMANCE ACCURACY based on spike rate alone, and spike count per 2 s IS NOT AN OPTIMAL NEURAL SIGNAL for coding sound shape
span.quote: All three cortical fields classify sounds with a low performance accuracy based on spike rate alone ( Fig. 8 E–G ). Accordingly, on average A1 neurons have near chance levels of performance (i.e., <15%) across all sound shapes ( Fig. 8 H , blue line). In VAF and cSRAF, spike rate-based classification accuracy is only significantly higher for the sound burst with the longest half-duration (80 ms, f c of 2 Hz; Fig. 8 H , asterisk; p < 0.05). These results suggest that spike count or equivalent spike rate per 2 s is not an optimal neural signal for coding sound shape in primary and non-primary auditory cortices.

span.label: and pooling does not rescue it - pooled spike-rate classification is CLOSE TO CHANCE LEVELS in all cortical fields, while the timing-based classifier reaches 80 to 100%
span.quote: In contrast, the pooled output performance is close to chance levels when we use a spike-rate-based sound classifier in all cortical fields ( Fig. 8 L , dotted lines, M–O ). Nevertheless, classification performance significantly varies with the method of classification (spike timing vs rate, A1: F (9,980) = 144.2, p = 0; VAF: F (9,980) = 144.37, p = 0; SRAF: F (9,980) = 301.03, p = 0, two-way ANOVA) and across cortical fields (A1: F (1,980) = 9362.78, p = 0; VAF: F (1,980) = 7758.69, p = 0; SRAF: F (1,980) = 4934.89, p = 0, two-way ANOVA). These results indicate that spike timing provides a robust signal for sound shape classification and performance improves when output from more neurons can be pooled to classify sounds.

span.label: with the number of neurons needed stated per field: HALF MAXIMAL PERFORMANCE from fewer than 10 neurons everywhere, but A1 and VAF require 3 and 5 against 16 for cSRAF
span.quote: Half maximal performance is achieved when pooling output from small (<10) populations of neurons for spike-timing-based classification in all cortices. Importantly, A1 and VAF require fewer neurons (3 and 5 respectfully) than cSRAF (16 neurons) and cSRAF converges less rapidly to achieve half maximal sound classification than A1 and VAF

span.label: and a resolution limit read off the point where performance drops - a HALF-RESOLUTION LIMIT ON THE ORDER OF 20 ms
span.quote: Discrimination performance drops ( p < 0.05, f c ( F (8,1323) = 44.8, two-way ANOVA) for sounds with half-durations shorter than 28 ms (shape f c ≥ 8 Hz) when the reference sound half-duration is 2 ms ( f c of 64 Hz) suggesting a half-resolution limit on the order of 20 ms

span.label: THE HIERARCHY IS CLAIMED AS DIRECTIONAL: non-primary cortex COULD CERTAINLY POOL RESPONSES FROM A1 to classify sounds BUT THE REVERSE IS LESS LIKELY, and structures reading cSRAF would need longer integration times than structures reading A1
span.quote: A hierarchy in time scales between A1 and non-primary cortices may reflect functional hierarchies for pooling, decoding and classifying sounds. The degree of sound classification performance improvement with neuron response pooling is robust in A1 and cSRAF for short ( Table 2 ; f c > 8 Hz) and longer ( Table 2 ; f c < 8 Hz, half-durations ≥20 ms) duration sound bursts, respectively. Thus, cortices may have distinct optimal time scales for pooling and decoding cortical responses in much the same way that they have distinct optimal time scales for pairwise sound burst discriminations. Accordingly, brain structures that receive and pool output from cSRAF could require longer temporal integration times than structures that pool output from A1. In such a scenario, non-primary cortex could certainly pool responses from A1 to classify sounds but the reverse is less likely.

span.label: A CONCEPT MOVED FROM SPACE TO TIME, AGAIN: functional hierarchies IN THE VISUAL CORTICES support the concept that classifying objects requires successive stages with a PROGRESSIVE INCREASE IN RECEPTIVE FIELD SIZE, and this study supports the idea that A SIMILAR PROGRESSION EXISTS IN AUDITORY CORTICES IN THE TIME DOMAIN
span.quote: Functional hierarchies in the visual cortices support the concept that classification of visual objects requires successive cortical stages of processing including a progressive increase in classical receptive field size. The present study is significant as it supports the idea that a similar progression exists in auditory cortices in the time domain. We demonstrate for the first time that three cortices provide temporal spiking patterns for robust temporal envelope shape discrimination but only the ventral non-primary cortices do so on long time scales.

span.label: and the specialisation is framed as a trade-off rather than a ranking: A1 has SUPERIOR TEMPORAL RESOLUTION AT THE EXPENSE OF SPECTRAL RESOLUTION, and the non-primary fields the reverse
span.quote: It is possible these specializations reflect time-frequency tradeoffs in sound processing where A1, and its corresponding thalamocortical pathway, have superior temporal resolution at the expense of spectral resolution. Conversely, non-primary fields, and corresponding thalamocortical pathways, could be better at resolving frequency cues at the expense of resolving timing cues.

span.label: extends → Phillips et al., 2002; Heil, 2003; Zheng and Escabí, 2013; Lee et al., 2016
span.quote: This study finds cortical neuron population response delays and durations change with the temporal shape of the sound envelope, providing a potential neural code and extending prior studies in midbrain and A1 ( Phillips et al., 2002 ; Heil, 2003 ; Zheng and Escabí, 2013 ) and non-primary auditory cortex ( Lee et al., 2016 ).

span.label: replicates → Malone et al., 2015 (A1 response duration versus sound burst duration)
span.quote: Because duration of the sound burst decreases with increasing f c in our sounds (see Materials and Methods), this result is consistent with prior observations in A1 ( Malone et al., 2015 ).

span.label: builds-on → Larson et al., 2009 (robustness of pairwise discrimination to response jitter)
span.quote: This supports the concept that pairwise discriminations are robust to differences in response duration or jitter, as reported previously ( Larson et al., 2009 ).

span.label: builds-on → Van Rossum (2001) spike-distance metric
span.quote: Our metric is motivated by the spike-distance metric of Van Rossum (2001) , which uses an exponential smoothing kernel to change the temporal resolution for integrating spikes in spike trains.

span.label: extends → prior work showing that response duration tracks sound envelope shape in A1, by measuring the same thing in two non-primary fields
span.quote: Across all sound conditions the average response duration increases significantly ( p < 0.001) and in rank order with: A1 < VAF < cSRAF ( Fig. 2 F ). These results indicate that response duration varies in a distinct manner from response peak delay. Moreover, response duration could encode the slope and/or duration of the sound burst envelope in all three cortical fields and the time scale for such encoding increases logarithmically and in a hierarchical fashion as one moves ventral from A1 to non-primary cortex.

span.label: contradicts → the reading that a longer time scale means better sound coding - the field with the longest time scale classifies worst
span.quote: Here, we provide additional evidence that the ability to classify 10 sound shapes with spike-timing pattern is inversely related to the temporal imprecision of cortical responses with: A1 > VAF > cSRAF. Thus, cSRAF typically has weak onset and longer duration responses with correspondingly less accurate sound classification performance with the temporal-code-based classifier ( Fig. 8 P , solid lines). Conversely, cSRAF has a slightly more robust performance with the rate-code-based classifier

span.label: supports → a spike-timing code over a spike-rate code, since rate classification stays near chance even when pooled
span.quote: In contrast, the pooled output performance is close to chance levels when we use a spike-rate-based sound classifier in all cortical fields ( Fig. 8 L , dotted lines, M–O ). Nevertheless, classification performance significantly varies with the method of classification (spike timing vs rate, A1: F (9,980) = 144.2, p = 0; VAF: F (9,980) = 144.37, p = 0; SRAF: F (9,980) = 301.03, p = 0, two-way ANOVA) and across cortical fields (A1: F (1,980) = 9362.78, p = 0; VAF: F (1,980) = 7758.69, p = 0; SRAF: F (1,980) = 4934.89, p = 0, two-way ANOVA). span.label: onset spikes alone discriminate sound shape well in all three fields, WHEREAS SUSTAINED RESPONSES PROVIDE MORE EFFECTIVE DISCRIMINATION IN NON-PRIMARY CORTICES

In all three cortical fields, discrimination performance is generally lower when only the secondary spikes are used to estimate sound shape discrimination ( Fig. 7 E–G vs A–C ). However, VAF and cSRAF outperform A1 when only these secondary spikes are used ( Fig. 7 H , asterisks). These results support the idea that onset responses strongly contribute to neural discrimination of sound shape in all cortical fields; whereas, sustained responses provide more effective discrimination in non-primary cortices, VAF and cSRAF.

span.label: non-primary cortex COULD CERTAINLY POOL RESPONSES FROM A1 to classify sounds BUT THE REVERSE IS LESS LIKELY
span.quote: A hierarchy in time scales between A1 and non-primary cortices may reflect functional hierarchies for pooling, decoding and classifying sounds. The degree of sound classification performance improvement with neuron response pooling is robust in A1 and cSRAF for short ( Table 2 ; f c > 8 Hz) and longer ( Table 2 ; f c < 8 Hz, half-durations ≥20 ms) duration sound bursts, respectively. Thus, cortices may have distinct optimal time scales for pooling and decoding cortical responses in much the same way that they have distinct optimal time scales for pairwise sound burst discriminations. Accordingly, brain structures that receive and pool output from cSRAF could require longer temporal integration times than structures that pool output from A1. In such a scenario, non-primary cortex could certainly pool responses from A1 to classify sounds but the reverse is less likely.

span.quote: The exponential time constant, τ, determines the temporal resolution or integration time of the distance metric. For large values of τ, the signals being compared contain mostly slow fluctuations in the spike rate ( Fig. 3 E , F ). For small τ, the spike distance metric is sensitive to the precise timing of spikes. We varied τ in 16 logarithmic intervals from 1 to 256 ms, and computed discrimination index ( D′ ) for each τ and each reference sound ( Fig. 4 ; reference sound f c = 64 Hz) and then determined the time constant (τ or tau) that yields the optimal (aka, maximal) sound discrimination ( Fig. 4 , asterisks). The same approach was used for all possible sound pairings and sound references and discrimination indices are plotted in a matrix ( Fig. 5 ). A discrimination index of zero was obtained when the two response conditions were identical (aka, sound vs itself) and plotted on the diagonal of the corresponding discrimination index matrix ( Fig. 5 , diagonal cells). Using a τ of 256 ms, the time constant is longer than half of the cycle period (500 ms), and the spike distance is closely related to the difference in the total spike rates. The range of time-constants tested enabled us to test the role precise spike timing at one extreme and the role of slow fluctuations in spike rate at the other extreme might play for neural discrimination of temporal envelope cues.

span.quote: As τ approaches the total length of the spike train (2 s), the spike distance is biased and yields large values. When comparing two spike trains, slight difference in the spike rate will contribute to a large spike-distance metric because there is not enough time for the exponential function to decay. To minimize this confound, we extended the length of spike train by synthesizing a periodic spike train with matched temporal statistics to the measured data ( Zheng and Escabí, 2008 ). For each cycle of the synthetic periodic spike train, both the spike rate and spike times were randomly sampled from the original spike train. This process was repeated to generate periodic spike trains with durations of 100 s.
